\section[\hi{घंटा}]{\hi{घंटा} — "hour," literally "bell"}

\label{lesson:HI-C18-ghanta}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Here's a word that wears its history on its sleeve: Hindi's word for "hour" is the exact same word as "bell."
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{घंटा} — bell AND hour, one word}
\textbf{\hi{घंटा}} (\emph{ghanṭā}) = "\textbf{hour}" — and it means "\textbf{bell, gong}" just as commonly. It comes from Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{घण्टा}} (\emph{ghaṇṭā}), "bell, gong." The connection isn't a coincidence: temples, towns, and later clock towers historically marked the passing of time by \textbf{striking a bell} — the hour was announced by sound, not read off a face — so the word for the bell itself came to mean the unit of time it announced. Compare this to English \textbf{o'clock}, itself a worn-down "\textbf{of the clock}," or French's \textbf{il est … heures}: different languages, but time-telling vocabulary keeps circling back to the \emph{instrument} used to mark it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \hi{बजना} — "to strike, to toll"}]
Hindi tells the time with the verb \textbf{\hi{बजना}} (\emph{bajnā}), "\textbf{to strike, to toll}" — the same imagery as a bell striking the hour:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{एक} \hi{बज} \hi{रहा} \hi{है।}} — "It is one o'clock." (literally "\textbf{one is striking}") \textbf{\hi{दो} \hi{बज} \hi{रहे} \hi{हैं।}} — "It is two o'clock." (literally "\textbf{two are striking}")
\end{quote}

Just like Spanish switches from singular \emph{es} to plural \emph{son} after "one," Hindi switches \textbf{\hi{बज} \hi{रहा} \hi{है}} (singular) to \textbf{\hi{बज} \hi{रहे} \hi{हैं}} (plural) once the count passes one — matching the number, not just tacking on "o'clock."
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ghanṭā" — hour, also "bell"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ek baj raha hai" — it is one o'clock, "one is striking"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "do baj rahe hain" — it is two o'clock, "two are striking"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\hi{घंटा}} literally mean besides "hour"? (\textbf{"Bell, gong"} — from Sanskrit \emph{ghaṇṭā}.) Why did "bell" come to mean "hour"? (Because clocks/towns historically \textbf{struck a bell} to announce the hour.) What verb does Hindi use to tell the time, and what does it literally mean? (\textbf{\hi{बजना}}, \emph{bajnā} — "to strike, to toll," as in \emph{ek baj raha hai}, "one is striking.")
\end{tcolorbox}
